\title{When does shrinkage beat the average star rating? A preregistered
simulation of rank recovery under noise, sparsity and misspecification}
\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\textbf{Author:} Mohamed Bechir Kefi, independent researcher.

\textbf{Status:} independent research manuscript / preprint draft, not
peer-reviewed. Version M4, 2026-11-25. Protocol v1.0 frozen by the owner
on 2026-11-24 before any confirmatory run.

\textbf{Data:} all results are simulated. Two simulation parameters are
calibrated on MovieLens 1M (Harper and Konstan 2015), which is not
redistributed. Real product quality is unobserved, and nothing here
describes any commercial platform or labels any review.

\section{Abstract}\label{abstract}

Sorting products by their average star rating favours items with few
reviews; Bayesian averages and lower credible bounds are common
remedies. How much they change the recovered order, and when, is less
clear. In a preregistered simulation where the true quality of 200
products is known by construction, we compared the arithmetic mean
(MEAN) with a Bayesian average of five pseudo-reviews at the catalogue
mean (SHRINK\_5, primary arm), variants with one and twenty
pseudo-reviews, and a Dirichlet lower credible bound (LCB). The design
crossed review count, rating noise, reporting selection and
quality-dependent exposure, with 20 seeds per cell and four prespecified
sensitivity analyses (1,560 runs, none failed). The primary estimand,
the grid-average difference in Kendall tau-b between SHRINK\_5 and MEAN,
was 0.0046 (95\% interval 0.0030 to 0.0061), so the frozen rule declares
the primary hypothesis supported. Its sign depends on rating noise:
-0.0198 (-0.0225 to -0.0172) at 0.5 stars, 0.0085 (0.0056 to 0.0113) at
1.0 and 0.0250 (0.0224 to 0.0277) at 1.5. The advantage survives
removing unreviewed products but reverses when the shrinkage centre is
off by half a star or the quality distribution changes shape. The
predicted decline with review count was contradicted, and the LCB ranked
whole lists worse than MEAN. In the conditions tested, shrinkage helped
ranking when ratings were noisy and the prior matched the population,
and hurt it otherwise.

\textbf{Keywords:} rating aggregation; empirical Bayes shrinkage;
ranking under uncertainty; Kendall tau; simulation study;
preregistration.

\section{1. Introduction}\label{introduction}

Online catalogues commonly summarise each product by the arithmetic mean
of its star ratings and sort by that number. A product with one
five-star review then outranks a product with hundreds of reviews
averaging 4.8. Practitioner guidance has long pointed this out and
proposes two remedies: a Bayesian average, which adds pseudo-reviews at
a global mean (Miller 2012; Algolia, n.d.), and a lower bound on a
posterior or confidence interval (Miller 2009, 2014). The statistical
idea behind the first remedy, shrinking separate estimates towards a
common value, goes back at least to the empirical Bayes work of Efron
and Morris (Efron and Morris 1975).

These remedies are standard; this paper does not propose a new
estimator. The gap it addresses is narrower: whether, and under which
conditions, accounting for sample size improves the recovered
\textbf{order} of products, measured against a known truth, and how
sensitive that improvement is to the assumptions it rests on. Better
squared-error estimates do not automatically give a better ranking, and
a remedy that helps in one regime can hurt in another.

\textbf{Research question.} When do average ratings misrank products
compared with uncertainty-aware estimators?

\textbf{Hypotheses (frozen before data).} H1: the grid-average
rank-recovery advantage of SHRINK\_5 over MEAN is positive. H1b: the
advantage decreases as the mean review count grows, at every noise
level. H1c: the LCB also beats MEAN. H2 (nondirectional, exploratory in
intent): the advantage changes with reporting selection and with
quality-dependent exposure. Four sensitivity analyses could invalidate
the main interpretation.

\textbf{Contributions.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A preregistered simulation design, frozen by the owner with file
  hashes before any confirmatory output, with prespecified decision
  rules and invalidation criteria (section 4).
\item
  A complete set of confirmatory results, including the contradicted and
  unsupported hypotheses and two triggered invalidation criteria
  (section 5).
\item
  Evidence that, under this model, the sign of the shrinkage advantage
  is set by rating noise and that the advantage is fragile to a
  misspecified shrinkage target or population shape (sections 5 and 6).
\item
  An open evidence chain: per-run provenance, checksums, a generator for
  every table and figure, and an audit that recomputes the frozen
  analysis from the raw results (section 10).
\end{enumerate}

\section{2. Related work}\label{related-work}

This is a scoping review, not a systematic one; the access status of
each source is listed in the references and in
\texttt{research/literature\_review.md}.

\textbf{Ranking by average rating.} Miller argues that sorting by a raw
average or by the difference of positive and negative votes misorders
items with few ratings, and proposes the lower bound of the Wilson score
interval for binary ratings (Miller 2009). For star ratings he proposes
a Dirichlet posterior over the five star levels and sorting by the
posterior mean minus a multiple of its standard deviation (Miller 2014);
our LCB arm follows that formula, with the prior recentred as described
in section 3. A related note frames the ranking criterion as the result
of an asymmetric loss chosen by the designer (Miller 2012). A
practitioner guide documents the Bayesian average
\((n\bar{x} + C m)/(n + C)\) as a common way to rank by rating (Algolia,
n.d.); it shows that SHRINK is current practice rather than a
contribution.

\textbf{Shrinkage.} Efron and Morris study Stein-type estimators that
shrink separate means towards a common value (Efron and Morris 1975).
Only the first page of that article was read for this project, so it is
cited for the general idea and not for any specific result. Whether
shrinkage improves the ordering of items, as opposed to their estimates,
is the question tested here.

\textbf{Selection in online ratings.} Hu, Pavlou and Zhang describe
purchasing and under-reporting biases that produce J-shaped rating
distributions and make the mean a biased estimator of quality (Hu,
Pavlou, and Zhang 2007); the full working paper was opened and this
statement was checked against its abstract and introduction, but the
paper was not read in full. Li and Hitt describe self-selection of early
reviewers (Li and Hitt 2008); this statement was checked against the
abstract and introduction of an author-hosted 2007 working-paper
version, not against the published article. These works motivate the
selection and exposure factors of EXP-002. They do not validate the
functional forms or parameter values used here.

\textbf{Relation to this study.} The study replicates no prior
experiment. It extends the practitioner argument by measuring, against a
known truth, the size and sign of the rank-recovery change and its
dependence on noise, sparsity, selection and prior misspecification.
Statistical work on ranking under uncertainty (for example posterior
expected ranks) was not searched, so we claim no novelty relative to it.

\section{3. Formal model}\label{formal-model}

All quantities are synthetic; protocol \texttt{research/protocol.md}
sections 2 to 5 gives the full definitions.

\textbf{Products and quality.} A catalogue has \(N = 200\) products.
Latent quality is \(\mu_i = 1 + 4B_i\) stars,
\(B_i \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\), with \((a, b) = (4.2726, 3.1944)\)
from the MovieLens fit (section 4.2).

\textbf{Ratings.} A potential rating is
\(r_{ij} = \mathrm{clip}(\lfloor \mu_i + \sigma \varepsilon_{ij} + 0.5 \rfloor, 1, 5)\)
with \(\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, 1)\), so \(\sigma\) is rating noise in
stars.

\textbf{Truth.} The ranking target is the expected rating
\(\theta_i = E[r_{ij} \mid \mu_i, \sigma] = \sum_{k=1}^{5} k \, P(r = k \mid \mu_i, \sigma)\),
computed exactly. For fixed \(\sigma\) it is strictly increasing in
\(\mu_i\).

\textbf{Review counts and exposure.} Potential raters follow
\(n^*_i \sim \mathrm{NegBin}(\text{mean } \nu w_i, \text{shape } r)\)
with \(r = 0.4909\) from the MovieLens fit, so zero reviews occur. The
exposure weight \(w_i = \exp(\gamma z_i) / \overline{\exp(\gamma z)}\),
with \(z_i\) the standardised \(\mu_i\), couples exposure to quality
when \(\gamma \neq 0\).

\textbf{Reporting selection.} A potential rating \(r\) is reported with
probability \(\pi(r) = (1 + \lambda |r - 3| / 2) / (1 + \lambda)\);
\(\lambda > 0\) under-reports moderate ratings.

\textbf{Estimators.} With \(n_i\) reported ratings of mean \(\bar{x}_i\)
and catalogue mean \(m\) of all reported ratings:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  MEAN: \(s_i = \bar{x}_i\), or \(m\) if \(n_i = 0\) (baseline).
\item
  SHRINK(\(\kappa\)):
  \(s_i = (n_i \bar{x}_i + \kappa m) / (n_i + \kappa)\),
  \(\kappa \in \{1, 5, 20\}\); \(\kappa = 5\) is the prespecified
  primary arm.
\item
  LCB: posterior mean minus \(1.645\) posterior standard deviations
  under a Dirichlet prior \(\alpha_k = 5 p_k\), where \(p_k\) is the
  catalogue share of star level \(k\) (amendment A-1: the prior has
  Miller's total strength of five pseudo-ratings but is centred on
  \(m\)).
\item
  ORACLE: \(s_i = \theta_i\) (implementation check only; must give tau-b
  = 1).
\end{itemize}

Ties in score are broken by product id; rank metrics use tau-b, which
treats ties explicitly.

\textbf{Primary metric and estimand.} Kendall tau-b between scores and
\(\theta\) over all 200 products. For one catalogue,
\(D = \tau_b(\text{SHRINK}_5) - \tau_b(\text{MEAN})\). The primary
estimand \(\bar{D}\) is the equal-weight mean over the nine EXP-001
cells of the per-cell expected \(D\). Amendment A-2 adds \(D_\sigma\),
the equal-weight mean of the three cells at each noise level. Secondary
metrics are Spearman's rho, precision at 10, regret at 10 (mean
\(\theta\) of the true top 10 minus that of the arm's top 10, in stars),
interval coverage and RMSE.

\textbf{Complexity.} Each estimator is linear in the number of ratings;
tau-b is computed in \(O(N \log N)\) and validated against an \(O(N^2)\)
reference. A full experiment runs in seconds on a laptop (section 4.5).

\section{4. Methods}\label{methods}

\subsection{4.1 Design and registration}\label{design-and-registration}

Three experiments were registered
(\texttt{research/experiment\_registry.csv}) and frozen by the owner on
2026-11-24 with SHA-256 hashes of the study protocol, the three
experiment protocols, seven configs and the data manifest
(\texttt{research/freeze.json}; decision D-010). A run guard refuses any
config whose hash differs from the freeze record.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{EXP-001 (primary).} Mean review count
  \(\nu \in \{3, 10, 30\}\) by noise \(\sigma \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5\}\);
  \(\lambda = 0\), \(\gamma = 0\); 9 cells, 20 seeds, 180 catalogues.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-002.} \(\lambda \in \{0, 2\}\) by
  \(\gamma \in \{-0.5, 0, 0.5\}\) by \(\nu \in \{3, 10\}\);
  \(\sigma = 1.0\); 12 cells, 240 catalogues.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-003 (sensitivity).} S1: metrics restricted to products
  with \(n_i \ge 1\) and, separately, \(n_i \ge 5\). S2: SHRINK\_5
  centred at \(m + 0.5\) and \(m - 0.5\). S3: truth \(\theta\) versus
  the expected reported rating \(\theta^{rep}\) on EXP-002 catalogues.
  S4: quality \(\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)\) and an equal mixture of
  \(\mathrm{Beta}(2, 6)\) and \(\mathrm{Beta}(6, 2)\). 1,140 catalogues.
\end{itemize}

All arms score the same catalogue (paired design). Seeds derive from
\texttt{SeedSequence({[}20261124,\ exp\_number,\ seed\_index{]})} with
separate streams for quality, counts, ratings and reporting, so a seed
shares its latent qualities across cells.

\subsection{4.2 Calibration on MovieLens
1M}\label{calibration-on-movielens-1m}

MovieLens 1M (1,000,209 ratings of 3,883 listed movies) was used for
calibration only (Harper and Konstan 2015); the data are fetched by
script and never committed. Movies were split once into a fit half
(1,941 movies) and a check half (1,942). On the fit half, a negative
binomial fitted by maximum likelihood gave the shape \(r = 0.49090\),
and a marginal maximum-likelihood fit of the model of section 3 gave
\(\mathrm{Beta}(4.27261, 3.19443)\) and a reference noise
\(\sigma = 1.05215\), which is not used (the noise grid is a design
factor). The fit computed no estimator, catalogue or contrast. On the
check half the model misfits the star shares: 1-star and 4-star shares
are under-predicted (0.078 and 0.268 predicted against 0.110 and 0.303
observed) and 2-star and 5-star shares over-predicted. The fitted values
entered the configs rounded to four decimals.

\subsection{4.3 Statistical analysis}\label{statistical-analysis}

Per cell, the mean paired difference has a 95\% percentile bootstrap
interval over seeds (10,000 resamples, fixed seed) with a t interval as
cross-check. Pooled quantities use a stratified bootstrap that resamples
seeds within cells. \textbf{H1} is supported if the one-sided 95\% lower
bound of \(\bar{D}\) is above 0. If the \(D_\sigma\) intervals exclude 0
with opposite signs, A-2 requires the result to be stated as ``the
direction depends on the noise level''. \textbf{H1b} is contradicted if
the order \(\nu = 3 > 10 > 30\) fails in a majority of noise levels or
the \(\nu = 3\) and \(\nu = 30\) intervals overlap at every level. The
secondary family (H1b contrast, H1c, SHRINK\_1 and SHRINK\_20 against
MEAN) uses Holm at \(\alpha = 0.05\). EXP-002 uses same-seed paired
differences of \(D\) between factor levels within strata, averaged with
equal weight, with Holm across the lambda and two gamma contrasts.
EXP-003 invalidation criteria are sign reversals (S2, S4), an interval
reaching 0 (S1) and sign differences in a majority of cells (S3).

The frozen text named Holm but no p-value; the analysis layer, committed
before any confirmatory catalogue existed, uses bootstrap p-values from
the same resamples (decision D-011, accepted by the owner with
disclosure, D-013).

\subsection{4.4 Confirmatory versus exploratory
work}\label{confirmatory-versus-exploratory-work}

Every result in section 5.1 to 5.3 is confirmatory. Before the freeze,
exploratory pilots under the planning generator were run; the freeze
record (\texttt{research/freeze.json}, item C4) lists the contrast
values seen. They showed the same sign change by noise and motivated
amendment A-2. The noise dependence reported below is therefore a
confirmatory replication of a pattern seen in pilots, not a prediction
made blind to it. Section 5.4 reports three post-hoc exploratory checks
made at M4 (journal JRN-0010); they never change a frozen verdict.

\subsection{4.5 Implementation, compute and
reproducibility}\label{implementation-compute-and-reproducibility}

Python 3.12.1 with numpy 2.3.4 and scipy 1.16.2, locked by
\texttt{uv.lock}; Apple M1 Pro, 16 GiB, macOS 15.3.1. All 1,560
confirmatory runs executed at revision \texttt{bd9e146} (clean tree) on
2026-11-24 between 23:35:19 and 23:35:48 UTC; EXP-001 took 2.22 s of
wall time. No run failed or was retried. Before the runs, the test suite
passed (165 tests), 26 of 26 metric-validation checks passed, and the
ORACLE arm gave tau-b = 1 in every confirmatory run.

\section{5. Results}\label{results}

All values are simulated and unitless (tau-b differences) unless stated.
Intervals are two-sided 95\% stratified bootstrap intervals.

\subsection{5.1 EXP-001: shrinkage versus the mean
(primary)}\label{exp-001-shrinkage-versus-the-mean-primary}

\textbf{H1.} \(\bar{D} = 0.0046\) (0.0030 to 0.0061), one-sided 95\%
lower bound 0.0032, nine cells: \textbf{supported} under the frozen
rule.

\textbf{Per noise level (A-2).} The three intervals exclude 0 with
opposite signs, so the frozen wording applies: \textbf{the direction
depends on the noise level} (Table 1, Figure 1).

\textbf{H1b: contradicted.} The decreasing order holds at one of three
noise levels, and at sigma 0.5 only because \(D\) becomes more negative.
At sigma 1.5, \(D\) increases with \(\nu\). Part of this increase is
dilution (section 5.4, E3).

\textbf{Secondary family (Holm).} SHRINK\_1 improves on MEAN: 0.0075
(0.0066 to 0.0082), Holm-adjusted p 0.0004. SHRINK\_20 is worse: -0.0125
(-0.0143 to -0.0106). \textbf{H1c is not supported}: LCB minus MEAN is
-0.0647 (-0.0689 to -0.0604), Holm-adjusted p 1.0000, and negative at
every noise level (-0.0953, -0.0581, -0.0406). The H1b contrast
(\(\nu = 3\) minus \(\nu = 30\)) is -0.0004 (-0.0042 to 0.0036). By
noise level, SHRINK\_1 is null at sigma 0.5 (-0.0001, -0.0017 to
0.0014), and SHRINK\_20 follows the sign pattern of SHRINK\_5 with a
larger low-noise loss (-0.0478 at sigma 0.5, 0.0183 at sigma 1.5).

\textbf{Realised sparsity.} The share of products with no review was
0.381, 0.220 and 0.132 at \(\nu\) = 3, 10 and 30.

\textbf{Selection.} Under-reporting of moderate ratings did not change
the SHRINK\_5 advantage on average, although it cut mean reported counts
by about a third (for example from 9.92 to 6.32 at \(\nu = 10\),
\(\gamma = 0\)). Two of six per-stratum intervals exclude 0, in opposite
directions (0.0036 and -0.0045), so the frozen contradiction rule
(``every stratum interval contains 0'') is formally not met. We read
this as no detected average difference and not as equivalence.

\textbf{Exposure.} Coupling exposure to quality lowered the SHRINK\_5
advantage in both directions. The protocol's mechanism predicted
opposite effects for \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\gamma < 0\); this was not
borne out for SHRINK\_5. LCB, which pushes data-poor products down
rather than to the middle, followed the predicted pattern: it gained
when well-exposed products were the good ones (\(\gamma = 0.5\)) and
lost in the reverse case.

\subsection{5.3 EXP-003: sensitivity analyses that could invalidate the
interpretation}\label{exp-003-sensitivity-analyses-that-could-invalidate-the-interpretation}

Table 3. EXP-003, pooled \(D\) against MEAN under each condition
(EXP-001 reference 0.0046). Source:
\texttt{research/experiments/EXP-003/results\_tables.md}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{S1.} The advantage is not an artefact of scoring unreviewed
  products: it is larger among reviewed products. It disappears once
  products with fewer than five reviews are removed, so it lives among
  products with one to four reviews.
\item
  \textbf{S2 and S4.} Both invalidation criteria are met. A half-star
  error in the shrinkage centre, or a uniform or bimodal quality
  population, turns the small advantage into a loss several times
  larger. Under S4 the advantage survives only at sigma 1.5 (0.0045,
  0.0012 to 0.0078, for Beta(1, 1); the mixture's interval at that level
  contains 0).
\item
  \textbf{S3.} The registered check cannot discriminate. Within a cell
  both truth definitions are strictly increasing in \(\mu\), so every
  rank-only metric is identical under the two; the tau-b values matched
  exactly in all 240 runs (D-012, accepted with disclosure, D-013). Its
  ``criterion not met'' carries no evidence.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{5.4 Exploratory checks at M4 (not
confirmatory)}\label{exploratory-checks-at-m4-not-confirmatory}

Three cheap checks, run after the confirmatory analysis and labelled
exploratory (JRN-0010; \texttt{results/exploratory/m4-sensitivity/}),
probe competing explanations the registered design left open.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{E1, other metrics.} On EXP-001, SHRINK\_5 minus MEAN has the
  same sign pattern on all five metrics: negative at sigma 0.5 and
  positive at 1.0 and 1.5 for Spearman, precision at 10, regret at 10
  and RMSE. For example, precision at 10 changes by -0.0850 (-0.1200 to
  -0.0500) at sigma 0.5 and +0.1500 (0.1133 to 0.1867) at sigma 1.5. The
  noise dependence is not a property of tau-b.
\item
  \textbf{E1, LCB.} LCB is worse than MEAN on tau-b, Spearman and RMSE
  at every noise level, but at sigma 1.5 it is better on precision at 10
  (+0.1067, 0.0717 to 0.1417) and on regret at 10 (lower by 0.2245
  stars, 0.1947 to 0.2540). Its pooled regret at 10 is lower than MEAN's
  by 0.0888 stars (0.0732 to 0.1045). H1c's failure is specific to
  whole-list recovery.
\item
  \textbf{E2, ties.} Regenerating the 180 EXP-001 catalogues reproduced
  the committed tau-b values exactly. The share of products tied under
  MEAN depends on review count (0.857, 0.673 and 0.452 in the sigma 0.5
  cells at \(\nu\) = 3, 10, 30) and hardly on noise (0.857, 0.847, 0.849
  at \(\nu = 3\)), so ties cannot explain why the sign of \(D\) follows
  noise.
\item
  \textbf{E3, dilution.} Among reviewed products (S1 catalogues), \(D\)
  at sigma 1.5 is 0.0426, 0.0414 and 0.0405 at \(\nu\) = 3, 10, 30:
  flat. This suggests that the increase with \(\nu\) seen in EXP-001 at
  sigma 1.5 comes largely from unreviewed products, which are tied under
  both arms and are more common at small \(\nu\). The two sets of values
  are computed over different product subsets, so this is an
  interpretation, not a decomposition.
\end{itemize}

E1 alone contains 30 uncorrected intervals; isolated favourable rows,
such as LCB's top-of-list gains at sigma 1.5, are hypotheses for a
registered follow-up, not findings.

\section{6. Discussion}\label{discussion}

\textbf{What the evidence supports.} Under this model, shrinking towards
the catalogue mean helps whole-list rank recovery when individual
ratings are noisy (sigma 1.0 and 1.5 stars) and hurts it when they are
precise (sigma 0.5). The pattern holds on tau-b by the frozen analysis
and, in an exploratory check (E1), on the four other metrics. It also
appears in RMSE, which has no ties, so it is not an artefact of how
tau-b treats tied MEAN scores. A bias-variance reading fits this
pattern: with precise ratings one or two reviews already place a product
well, so pulling it towards the middle mainly moves genuinely good or
bad products to the wrong place; with noisy ratings the variance
reduction dominates. This reading is model-dependent; no experiment
isolated the two terms.

\textbf{What the pooled result does not mean.} The positive \(\bar{D}\)
is an equal-weight average over three noise levels, two of which favour
shrinkage. A grid weighted towards precise ratings would give a negative
average. The registered rule declares H1 supported, and we report it as
such, but the informative statement is the conditional one. The
MovieLens reference noise (1.05 stars) lies near the middle level, but
it folds rater heterogeneity into noise and comes from movies, so it
does not locate real product catalogues on this axis.

\textbf{Fragility.} The advantage depends on the shrinkage target being
right and on the population looking like the prior. A half-star error in
the centre, or a uniform or bimodal quality distribution, reverses it,
with losses (-0.0406 to -0.0485 and -0.0210 to -0.0265) several times
larger in magnitude than the reference gain of 0.0046. Shrinkage
strength matters as well: one pseudo-review gained modestly everywhere
except at sigma 0.5, twenty pseudo-reviews lost overall. Within this
model, the choice of centre and strength is at least as consequential as
the choice to shrink.

\textbf{Review count.} The hypothesis that the advantage fades as
reviews accumulate was contradicted. The exploratory dilution check (E3)
suggests why the raw pattern looked reversed at high noise: much of the
measured change with \(\nu\) comes from unreviewed products, which both
arms score identically. Among reviewed products, the data show no clear
dependence on \(\nu\), which is consistent with S1: once evaluation is
restricted to products with at least five reviews the advantage
vanishes, so it arises from orderings that involve products with fewer
than five reviews. A plausible reading, not tested directly, is that
raising \(\nu\) mainly changes how many such products there are.

\textbf{The lower bound.} The centred LCB ranks the whole list worse
than the mean, as designed: it penalises uncertainty and so moves
data-poor products down regardless of their quality. On top-of-list
metrics at higher noise it did better than the mean in an exploratory
check, consistent with Miller's motivation of protecting the top of a
list (Miller 2014). Its strong reaction to exposure coupling (EXP-002)
shows that its behaviour depends on whether data-poor products are good
or bad, which a platform cannot observe directly.

\textbf{Selection.} Under-reporting of moderate ratings, in the stylised
form used here, did not change the shrinkage advantage on average.
Because at sigma 1.0 the advantage barely depends on review count, a
selection effect acting only through fewer reported ratings would also
be expected to be small, so the experiment cannot separate the two
explanations the protocol named.

\textbf{Relation to prior work.} The results agree with the practitioner
view that the raw mean is not a safe default in sparse, noisy data
(Miller 2009, 2014), and they qualify it: the same remedy can do harm
when ratings are precise or the prior is off. They do not test any claim
of the cited works directly.

\section{7. Limitations and threats to
validity}\label{limitations-and-threats-to-validity}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Simulation only.} True quality is defined by the model.
  Nothing here measures real product quality, and no result transfers to
  real platforms without further evidence.
\item
  \textbf{Model dependence.} Results depend on the quality distribution
  (S4 shows how much), the rounding and clipping rating model, negative
  binomial counts and the selection and exposure functions. Rounding and
  clipping near the scale ends were not separated from population shape.
  Herding and social influence, manipulation and rater heterogeneity are
  not modelled.
\item
  \textbf{Calibration transfer.} Dispersion and quality shape come from
  movie ratings with a mean of about 252 ratings per movie and are
  applied at 3 to 30. The single-noise model misfits held-out star
  shares.
\item
  \textbf{Grid dependence.} The pooled estimand weights three noise
  levels equally; its sign depends on that choice. EXP-002 ran at one
  noise level.
\item
  \textbf{Single points of misspecification.} S2 and S4 test one shift
  and two shapes; the size of misspecification at which the advantage
  disappears is not mapped.
\item
  \textbf{Non-diagnostic S3.} The registered truth-definition check
  cannot discriminate for rank metrics (D-012).
\item
  \textbf{Small effects.} The reference gain is 0.0046 tau-b units.
  Practical relevance at the top of a list was examined only in
  secondary and exploratory metrics.
\item
  \textbf{Estimator scope.} One LCB variant, three fixed shrinkage
  strengths; no learned or platform-specific ranking.
\item
  \textbf{Statistics.} Twenty seeds per cell; percentile bootstrap
  intervals agree closely with t intervals. Holm p-values use bootstrap
  tails (D-011). EXP-003 conditions are not corrected for multiplicity,
  as frozen. The per-noise contrasts are descriptive.
\item
  \textbf{Pre-freeze exposure.} The noise dependence was seen in
  exploratory pilots before the freeze (section 4.4).
\item
  \textbf{Scoping literature.} Several sources were read only in part
  (references); ranking-under-uncertainty literature in statistics was
  not searched.
\end{itemize}

\section{8. Ethics and responsible
research}\label{ethics-and-responsible-research}

The study uses simulated data and a public research dataset used for
calibration only, under its licence terms (research use, no
redistribution, citation required); the dataset is not committed or
redistributed. Only per-movie star counts were processed; user
demographics were never read and pseudonymous user ids were discarded
after a duplicate check. No human participants were involved and no
ethics approval was sought or claimed. Nothing in this work labels any
review as fraudulent, infers anything about real products, or describes
the internals of any commercial platform.

\section{9. Conclusion and future
work}\label{conclusion-and-future-work}

Under the frozen rule the primary hypothesis is supported, but the
supported statement is conditional: in this simulation, accounting for
sample size by shrinking towards the catalogue mean improves rank
recovery when individual ratings are noisy and degrades it when they are
precise, and the improvement reverses when the shrinkage target or the
population shape is misspecified. The predicted decline with review
count was contradicted, and the centred lower bound ranks whole lists
worse than the mean. Feasible follow-ups, each requiring a new
registered experiment and the owner's approval: a sigma-direction
hypothesis registered in advance; a map of the advantage over prior
shifts and population shapes; exposure and selection crossed with noise;
a value-based truth-definition check; and top-of-list metrics as a
primary outcome.
